newsitem.title: CANADA: Poll shows softening Liberal support in Ontario.
newsitem.headline: Poll shows softening Liberal support in Ontario.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien's ruling Liberals experienced a slide in support in vote-rich Ontario in the past three months, but still command a big lead in a new poll released on Friday.
The Decima Research poll, commissioned by the Global Television Network, found 28 percent of voters were committed Liberal supporters in the May 3-4 poll, down from 37 percent in early February.

Those leaning Liberal, however, rose by four points to 11 percent, and after apportioning those who would not answer, Decima calculated Liberal support at 55 percent of decided voters, to 19 percent for the Conservatives, 14 percent for the leftist New Democratic Party and 12 percent for Reform.
Ontario, Canada's richest and most populous province, is key to an election victory. It has 103 of the 301 seats in the next House of Commons.
The Liberals took 98 out 99 Ontario seats in 1993, largely because Conservative and Reform, both of whom now advocate tax cuts, split the right-wing vote.

The poll showed Conservative support (committed or leaning) falling to 14 percent from 16 percent among all those polled, the New Democrats steady at 10 percent and Reform growing two points to nine percent.
But 28 percent either were undecided, would not vote or would not answer.
Decima Executive Vice President David Crapper pointed to softening Liberal support as a sign that people were beginning to investigate the alternatives.
The poll surveyed 750 Ontarians and Decima said it had a margin of error of 3.58 percentage points, 19 times in 20.
